summary.text: Merge the three event-time families \(i\), \(i/x\), and \(i/y\), where \(x=\varphi/5\) and \(y=1/(5\varphi)\); irrationality makes all event times distinct, and the number at or below \(T\) is \(\lfloor T\rfloor+\lfloor Tx\rfloor+\lfloor Ty\rfloor\). Successive events therefore realize every positive rank exactly once, while evaluating the rank on each of the three families gives the corresponding floor formulas, yielding both coverage and pairwise disjointness.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad r=5,\qquad s=\varphi,\qquad t=\frac1\varphi.
\]
For positive integers \(n\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{n\varphi}{5}\right\rfloor
       +\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5\varphi}\right\rfloor,\\
b(n)&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{\varphi}\right\rfloor
       +\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\varphi^2}\right\rfloor,\\
c(n)&=n+\left\lfloor5n\varphi\right\rfloor
       +\left\lfloor n\varphi^2\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are respectively A207672, A207673, and A208326. Indeed, these formulas are exactly
\[
n+\lfloor ns/r\rfloor+\lfloor nt/r\rfloor,
\quad
n+\lfloor nr/s\rfloor+\lfloor nt/s\rfloor,
\quad
n+\lfloor nr/t\rfloor+\lfloor ns/t\rfloor,
\]
after substituting \(r=5\), \(s=\varphi\), and \(t=1/\varphi\). We prove that the three sets of values \(\{a(n):n\ge1\}\), \(\{b(n):n\ge1\}\), and \(\{c(n):n\ge1\}\) are pairwise disjoint and have union equal to the positive integers.

Set
\[
x=\frac{\varphi}{5},\qquad y=\frac{1}{5\varphi}.
\]
We shall jointly order three labeled families of positive real numbers. For every positive integer \(m\), introduce events
\[
A_m,\qquad B_m,\qquad C_m
\]
with respective event times
\[
\tau(A_m)=m,
\qquad
\tau(B_m)=\frac{m}{x},
\qquad
\tau(C_m)=\frac{m}{y}.
\]
Thus the three streams of event times are
\[
1,2,3,\ldots;
\qquad
\frac1x,\frac2x,\frac3x,\ldots;
\qquad
\frac1y,\frac2y,\frac3y,\ldots.
\]
The main idea is that \(a(m),b(m),c(m)\) will be precisely the positions occupied by \(A_m,B_m,C_m\), respectively, when all these events are placed in increasing order of their times.

We first establish that there are no ties among the labeled event times. The number \(\sqrt5\) is irrational: if \(\sqrt5=p/q\) with coprime positive integers \(p,q\), then \(p^2=5q^2\), so \(5\mid p\); writing \(p=5k\) then gives \(q^2=5k^2\), hence \(5\mid q\), contradicting coprimality. Consequently \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\) is irrational.

It follows that \(x=\varphi/5\) is irrational. Also \(y=1/(5\varphi)\) is irrational, since if it were rational, its nonzero reciprocal \(5\varphi\), and hence \(\varphi\), would be rational. Finally,
\[
\frac yx=\frac{1/(5\varphi)}{\varphi/5}=\frac1{\varphi^2}
\]
is irrational. To see this, recall the golden-ratio identity
\[
\varphi^2=\varphi+1.
\]
Thus \(\varphi^2\) is irrational, and the reciprocal of a nonzero irrational number cannot be rational, because a nonzero rational reciprocal would make the original number rational.

Now suppose an \(A\)-event and a \(B\)-event had equal times. Then for some positive integers \(m,n\),
\[
m=\frac n x,
\]
so \(mx=n\). This is impossible because a nonzero integer multiple of the irrational number \(x\) is irrational, whereas \(n\) is an integer. Similarly, equality \(\tau(A_m)=\tau(C_n)\) would give \(my=n\), which is impossible because \(y\) is irrational. Finally, equality \(\tau(B_m)=\tau(C_n)\) would give
\[
\frac m x=\frac n y,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
m\frac yx=n,
\]
which is impossible because \(y/x=1/\varphi^2\) is irrational. Within any one family, distinct indices plainly give distinct times, since \(x,y>0\). Therefore the event-time map is injective: two labeled events have equal times only when they are the same event.

For a nonnegative real number \(T\), let \(E(T)\) be the set of all labeled events whose times are at most \(T\). This set is finite. In the \(A\)-stream, the events at or below \(T\) are exactly those \(A_m\) with \(1\le m\le T\), so their number is \(\lfloor T\rfloor\). In the \(B\)-stream,
\[
\tau(B_m)=\frac m x\le T
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
m\le Tx,
\]
so there are \(\lfloor Tx\rfloor\) such events. Likewise there are \(\lfloor Ty\rfloor\) events from the \(C\)-stream. Since the three families are disjoint as labeled sets,
\[
|E(T)|=\lfloor T\rfloor+\lfloor Tx\rfloor+\lfloor Ty\rfloor.
\]
Define the counting function
\[
R(T)=\lfloor T\rfloor+\lfloor Tx\rfloor+\lfloor Ty\rfloor.
\]
Thus \(R(T)=|E(T)|\). In particular, for an event \(e\), the integer \(R(\tau(e))\) is its inclusive rank: it counts all events occurring no later than \(e\), including \(e\) itself.

We record two elementary consequences of this interpretation. First, if \(e\) and \(f\) are events with
\[
\tau(e)<\tau(f),
\]
then
\[
E(\tau(e))\subsetneq E(\tau(f)).
\]
The inclusion holds because every event no later than \(e\) is also no later than \(f\), and it is proper because \(f\) belongs to the second set but not the first. Hence
\[
R(\tau(e))<R(\tau(f)).
\]
Because distinct events have distinct times, it follows that distinct events have distinct ranks.

Second, every event has an immediate successor in the merged ordering. We give the argument carefully, since it ensures that no positive rank is skipped. Fix an event \(e\), and put
\[
M=\lfloor\tau(e)\rfloor+1.
\]
The \(A\)-event \(A_M\) occurs at time \(M\), and
\[
\tau(e)<M.
\]
Consider the events whose times lie in the interval \((\tau(e),M]\). This is a nonempty finite set: it is nonempty because it contains \(A_M\), and it is finite because it is contained in \(E(M)\). Choose from it an event \(f\) of smallest time. We claim that \(f\) is the least event later than \(e\) among all three infinite streams. Indeed, if an event \(g\) satisfies \(\tau(e)<\tau(g)\), then either \(\tau(g)\le M\), in which case minimality within the finite set gives \(\tau(f)\le\tau(g)\), or \(\tau(g)>M\), in which case \(\tau(f)\le M<\tau(g)\). Thus there is no event strictly between \(e\) and \(f\).

For such consecutive events \(e,f\), we have
\[
E(\tau(f))=E(\tau(e))\cup\{f\}.
\]
One inclusion is immediate. For the other, take an event \(g\) with \(\tau(g)\le\tau(f)\). If \(\tau(g)\le\tau(e)\), then \(g\in E(\tau(e))\). Otherwise \(\tau(e)<\tau(g)\), so the defining minimality of \(f\) gives \(\tau(f)\le\tau(g)\). Together with \(\tau(g)\le\tau(f)\), this yields equal times; injectivity of event times then gives \(g=f\). Also \(f\notin E(\tau(e))\). Taking cardinalities therefore gives
\[
R(\tau(f))=R(\tau(e))+1.
\]

We now prove that every positive integer occurs as the rank of exactly one event. First note that
\[
1<\varphi<2.
\]
Indeed, \(2<\sqrt5<3\), so \(3/2<\varphi<2\). In particular,
\[
0<x=\frac\varphi5<1.
\]
Also \(\varphi>1\), so
\[
0<y=\frac1{5\varphi}<1.
\]
The event \(A_1\) has time \(1\), and hence
\[
R(\tau(A_1))=R(1)
=\lfloor1\rfloor+\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor
=1+0+0=1.
\]
Starting from \(A_1\), repeatedly choose the immediate successor just constructed. At every step the rank rises by exactly one. Induction therefore shows that, for each positive integer \(N\), there is an event \(e\) with
\[
R(\tau(e))=N.
\]
Moreover, as shown above, distinct events have distinct ranks, so this event is unique.

It remains to identify the ranks of the three kinds of events with the three given sequences.

For an \(A\)-event, \(\tau(A_n)=n\), and therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(\tau(A_n))
&=\lfloor n\rfloor+\lfloor nx\rfloor+\lfloor ny\rfloor\\
&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{n\varphi}{5}\right\rfloor
    +\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5\varphi}\right\rfloor\\
&=a(n).
\end{aligned}
\]

For a \(B\)-event, \(\tau(B_n)=n/x\). Hence
\[
R(\tau(B_n))
=\left\lfloor\frac n x\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac n x x\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac n x y\right\rfloor.
\]
Since \(x=\varphi/5\), \(y/x=1/\varphi^2\), and \((n/x)x=n\), this becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(\tau(B_n))
&=\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{\varphi}\right\rfloor+n
  +\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\varphi^2}\right\rfloor\\
&=b(n).
\end{aligned}
\]

For a \(C\)-event, \(\tau(C_n)=n/y\). Therefore
\[
R(\tau(C_n))
=\left\lfloor\frac n y\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac n y x\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac n y y\right\rfloor.
\]
Now
\[
\frac1y=5\varphi,
\qquad
\frac xy
=\frac{\varphi/5}{1/(5\varphi)}=\varphi^2,
\qquad
\frac n y y=n.
\]
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(\tau(C_n))
&=\lfloor5n\varphi\rfloor
  +\lfloor n\varphi^2\rfloor+n\\
&=c(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the rank occupied by every event is a value of exactly the sequence corresponding to its label.

We can now conclude both parts of the partition assertion. Let \(N\) be any positive integer. There is an event of rank \(N\). It is necessarily of exactly one of the forms \(A_n,B_n,C_n\), so by the three rank identities,
\[
N=a(n),\quad N=b(n),\quad\text{or}\quad N=c(n)
\]
for some positive integer \(n\). Hence the union of the three ranges contains every positive integer. Conversely, every value of any of the three sequences is the rank of an event, and every such rank is positive because it counts at least the event itself. Thus their union is exactly the positive integers.

Finally, suppose that a number belonged to two of the three ranges, for example \(a(m)=b(n)\). The rank identities would say that the two distinct labeled events \(A_m\) and \(B_n\) have the same rank, contrary to the fact that distinct events have distinct ranks. The same argument applies to a putative equality \(a(m)=c(n)\) or \(b(m)=c(n)\). Therefore the three ranges are pairwise disjoint.

Hence A207672, A207673, and A208326 partition the positive integers.
